prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) --     More than 5,000 patients of a South Dakota urology clinic may have been exposed to hepatitis and HIV when the facility reused single-use medical products, state health officials said Friday. Clinic workers told inspectors they've been reusing products since the clinic opened its doors in 2002. The Siouxland Urology Center in Dakota Dunes has been ordered to contact nearly 5,700 former patients treated there since 2002. A routine inspection found the facility was reusing sterile saline bags, tubing and other medical supplies from cystoscopies -- a diagnostic procedure that looks at the lower urinary tract. "We witnessed the practice while we were in the facility," during a January inspection, said Barb Buhler of the South Dakota Health Department. Siouxland Urology has since been put under a provisional license and has been very cooperative, according to state officials. "Siouxland Urology Center informed certain of its patients by U.S. mail that a prior cystoscopy procedure could have potentially exposed them to an infectious disease," the facility's Web site said. It added that "the risk of infection from our past procedure is very minimal and we are unaware of any blood infections in our patients caused by the cystoscopy practice." The clinic, which primarily serves clients from South Dakota, Iowa and Nebraska, is offering free blood tests to those possibly affected to rule out the presence of viruses .Watch more on the possible exposure of urology patients » . On January 21, South Dakota Department of Health inspectors entered an examining room where a cystoscopy was about to take place, and noticed that a saline bag, which was hanging on a pole, was dated January 19, said Bob Stahl, of the South Dakota Department of Health. The inspectors, who are registered nurses, questioned the clinic staff. The clinic staff said they routinely reused saline bags and tubing, although both are clearly marked "for single use only," Stahl said. "They used the bags and tubing on multiple patients," Stahl said. He said the workers at the clinic told the inspectors they'd been reusing bags and tubing since the clinic opened in 2002. They said they didn't see anything wrong with the practice, Stahl said. "It was their standard operating procedure," Stahl said. "They told the inspectors that this was a common practice all over the country. We disagreed and told them this was not a common practice." He said that the clinic had been inspected seven times since it opened, and no one had noticed that the clinic was reusing equipment. "It was just by chance that this saline bag was hanging there. We run across these things by luck at times," Stahl said. "We're fortunate that the team was able to identify this." Fluids from patients can retreat into saline bags and tubing while the equipment is used, and reusing the tubing or saline bags could put patients at risk for contacting diseases from previous patients. A 1-liter bag of saline and tubing costs about $4, according to Mary Jo Lallis, account manager for PSS World Medical, Inc., a medical supply company. CNN's Greg Morrison and Elizabeth Cohen contributed to this report.

Clinic employees told inspectors that the products had been reused since the Siouxland Urology Center in Dakota Dunes opened in 2002. The center has been ordered to contact nearly 5,700 former patients treated there since that year.

During a routine inspection, officials discovered that the facility was reusing sterile saline bags, tubing, and other medical supplies during cystoscopies—a diagnostic procedure used to examine the lower urinary tract.

“We witnessed the practice while we were in the facility” during a January inspection, said Barb Buhler of the South Dakota Department of Health.

According to state officials, Siouxland Urology has since been placed under a provisional license and has been very cooperative.

“Siouxland Urology Center informed certain of its patients by U.S. mail that a prior cystoscopy procedure could have potentially exposed them to an infectious disease,” the facility said on its website.

It added that “the risk of infection from our past procedure is very minimal and we are unaware of any blood infections in our patients caused by the cystoscopy practice.”

The clinic, which primarily serves patients from South Dakota, Iowa, and Nebraska, is offering free blood tests to those who may have been affected to rule out the presence of viruses. *Watch more on the possible exposure of urology patients »*

On January 21, inspectors from the South Dakota Department of Health entered an examination room where a cystoscopy was about to take place and noticed that a saline bag hanging from a pole was dated January 19, said Bob Stahl of the department.

The inspectors, who are registered nurses, questioned clinic staff. Employees said they routinely reused saline bags and tubing, even though both were clearly labeled “for single use only,” Stahl said.

“They used the bags and tubing on multiple patients,” Stahl said.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — South Dakota health authorities said Friday that more than 5,000 people treated at a urology clinic may have faced possible exposure to HIV and hepatitis because staff repeatedly used medical supplies intended for only one patient.

Employees told investigators that the practice had continued since Siouxland Urology Center opened in Dakota Dunes in 2002. The clinic has been directed to notify almost 5,700 former patients who received care there from 2002 onward.

During a standard inspection, officials discovered that sterile saline bags, tubing and additional supplies used in cystoscopies were being used for multiple patients. A cystoscopy is a diagnostic examination of the lower urinary tract.

Barb Buhler of the South Dakota Department of Health said inspectors personally observed the practice during a January visit. State officials said Siouxland Urology was subsequently placed on a provisional license and has cooperated fully.

On its website, the center said it had mailed notices to some patients explaining that an earlier cystoscopy might have exposed them to an infectious illness. The clinic also stated that the likelihood of infection from its former procedure was extremely low and that it knew of no patient blood infections resulting from the way cystoscopies had been performed.

The facility mainly treats patients from South Dakota, Iowa and Nebraska. It is providing free blood testing to people who may have been affected so that viral infections can be ruled out.

Bob Stahl of the South Dakota Department of Health said inspectors entered an exam room on January 21 as staff were preparing to conduct a cystoscopy. They saw a saline bag suspended from a pole that carried a January 19 date. The inspectors, who are registered nurses, then questioned clinic personnel.

According to Stahl, employees acknowledged that they regularly used the same saline bags and tubing for more than one patient, despite labels stating that the products were for single use only. Staff members said this had been done since the center began operating in 2002 and indicated that they did not consider the practice improper.

Stahl described the reuse as part of the clinic’s normal procedures. He said workers claimed that facilities across the country commonly did the same thing, but inspectors rejected that assertion and told them it was not a widespread practice.

Although the center had undergone seven inspections since opening, the reuse of supplies had not previously been detected. Stahl said the discovery happened because the dated saline bag happened to be visible, adding that inspectors sometimes uncover such problems by chance and that it was fortunate the team recognized this one.

When the equipment is in operation, patient fluids can flow backward into the saline bag and tubing. Using those items again could therefore expose later patients to diseases carried by earlier ones.

Mary Jo Lallis, an account manager with medical-supply company PSS World Medical Inc., said a one-liter saline bag with tubing costs approximately $4.

CNN’s Greg Morrison and Elizabeth Cohen contributed to the report.

Employees reported that sterile saline bags, tubing, and other supplies used during cystoscopy procedures had been routinely reused since the facility opened in 2002.

The unsafe practice came to light during a January inspection, when inspectors directly observed staff reusing single-use equipment. As a result, the clinic was placed under a provisional license, and South Dakota health officials ordered it to notify nearly 5,700 former patients who had received treatment since 2002.

Siouxland Urology maintained that the risk of infection was minimal and said it was not aware of any related blood-borne infections. Nevertheless, the clinic offered free blood testing to patients who may have been affected, including screening for hepatitis and HIV.
outputs.L4:
A routine state inspection uncovered serious infection-control violations at Siouxland Urology Center, where staff had been reusing medical supplies labeled for single use during cystoscopy procedures. The practice reportedly dated back to 2002 and involved saline bags, tubing, and other equipment that should have been discarded after each patient.

Because reused supplies may allow blood-borne pathogens to pass from one patient to another, health officials determined that nearly 5,700 people could have been exposed to hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or HIV. Although no infections were known to have resulted from the violations, officials emphasized that the clinic’s procedures created an avoidable risk of cross-contamination.

The clinic was placed under a provisional license while it corrected its infection-control practices and demonstrated compliance with state standards. It was also ordered to identify and notify affected patients and to provide blood testing at no cost. Patients were encouraged to undergo testing even if they had no symptoms, since blood-borne infections can remain undetected for years.

The incident highlighted the importance of following manufacturers’ instructions and disposing of single-use medical products after every procedure. It also raised concerns about how unsafe practices could continue for years without being identified, underscoring the need for effective staff training, oversight, and regular infection-control monitoring.
